solution: \(x^2 y \cdot dx - (x^3 + y^3) \cdot dy = 0\). Therefore \(x^2 y - (x^3 + y^3) \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\) ... (I). This is homogeneous Differential equation. Put \(y = vx\) ... (II). Differentiate w. r. t. x, we get \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x \dfrac{dv}{dx}\) ... (III). Put (II) and (III) in Eq. (I), it becomes, \(x^2 \cdot vx - (x^3 + v^3 x^3)\left(v + x \dfrac{dv}{dx}\right) = 0\). Divide by \(x^3\), we get \(v - (1 + v^3)\left(v + x \dfrac{dv}{dx}\right) = 0\). Therefore \(v - v - x \dfrac{dv}{dx} - v^4 - v^3 x \dfrac{dv}{dx} = 0\). Therefore \(-x(1 + v^3) \dfrac{dv}{dx} = v^4\). Therefore \(\dfrac{1 + v^3}{v^4} \cdot dv = -\dfrac{dx}{x}\). Therefore \(\left(\dfrac{1}{v^4} + \dfrac{v^3}{v^4}\right) dv + \dfrac{dx}{x} = 0\). Integrating eq., we get \(\int v^{-4} dv + \int \dfrac{dv}{v} + \int \dfrac{dx}{x} = c_1\). Therefore \(\dfrac{v^{-3}}{-3} + \log(v) + \log(x) = c_1\). Therefore \(\log(vx) = c_1 + \dfrac{v^{-3}}{3}\), therefore \(\log(y) = c_1 + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{v^{-3}}{x^{-3}}\). Therefore \(3 \log(y) = 3 c_1 + \dfrac{x^3}{y^3}\). Therefore \(3 \log y = \dfrac{x^3}{y^3} + c\), where \(c = 3 c_1\).
note: Splitting (1 + v^3)/v^4 gives 1/v^4 + v^3/v^4; the line printed a minus sign (the next line integrates +dv/v).

solution: Let \(P(x, y)\) be any point on the curve \(y = f(x)\). The slope of the tangent at point \(P(x, y)\) is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Therefore \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y + 2x\). Therefore \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 2x\). This is linear differential equation of the type \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\) where \(P = -1\), \(Q = 2x\). Its solution is \(y \, (\text{I.F.}) = \int Q \cdot (\text{I.F.}) \, dx + c\) ... (I) where I.F. \(= e^{\int P dx} = e^{\int -dx} = e^{-x}\). eq. (I) becomes, \(y \cdot e^{-x} = \int 2x \times e^{-x} \, dx + c\). Therefore \(y \cdot e^{-x} = 2 \int x e^{-x} \, dx + c\) ... (II). Consider, \(\int x e^{-x} \, dx = x \int e^{-x} \, dx - \int \left(1 \times \dfrac{e^{-x}}{-1}\right) dx = \dfrac{x e^{-x}}{-1} + \int e^{-x} \, dx = -x e^{-x} + \int e^{-x} \, dx = -x e^{-x} - e^{-x} + c\). (II) becomes \(y \cdot e^{-x} = 2[-x e^{-x} - e^{-x}] + c\). Therefore \(y = -2x - 2 + c e^{x}\) ... (III). The curve passes through the origin \((0, 0)\). Therefore \(0 = -2(0) - 2 + c e^0\). Therefore \(0 = -2 + c\). Therefore \(2 = c\). Put in (III). Therefore \(y = -2x - 2 + 2 e^{x}\). Therefore \(2x + y + 2 = 2 e^{x}\) is the equation of the curve.
note: Multiplying y e^{-x} = 2(-x e^{-x} - e^{-x}) + c by e^{x} gives c e^{x}, not c e^{-x}; the curve is 2x + y + 2 = 2e^{x}, which satisfies dy/dx = y + 2x (the printed e^{-x} does not).

solution:
Let \(C(0, b)\) be the centre of the circle touching X-axis at the origin \((b > 0)\).

The radius of the circle is \(b\).

The equation of the circle is

\((x - 0)^2 + (y - b)^2 = b^2\)

\(\therefore x^2 + y^2 - 2by + b^2 = b^2\)

\(\therefore x^2 + y^2 - 2by = 0\) ... (I)

Differentiate w. r. t. x, we get

\(2x + 2y\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) - 2b\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0\)

\(\therefore x + (y - b)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{x}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)} + (y - b) = 0\)

\(\therefore b = y + \dfrac{x}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}\) ... (II)

From eq. (I) and eq. (II)

\(\therefore x^2 + y^2 - 2\left[y + \dfrac{x}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}\right]y = 0\)

\(\therefore x^2 + y^2 - 2y^2 - \dfrac{2xy}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)} = 0\)

\(\therefore x^2 - y^2 = \dfrac{2xy}{\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}\)

\(\therefore (x^2 - y^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2xy\)

is the required differential equation.
note: A circle touching the X-axis at the origin has its centre on the Y-axis, (0, b); with radius b, b > 0 (the line printed c(a, b) and b < 0).

solution:
[Textbook misprint: the first term should be \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) (Cauchy-Euler form), not \(x\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).]

We verify that \(y = 3\cos(\log x) + 4\sin(\log x)\) is a solution of \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\).

(Note: the standard form of this equation is \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\); we work with that.)

Differentiate:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -3\sin(\log x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} + 4\cos(\log x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x}\left[-3\sin(\log x) + 4\cos(\log x)\right]\).

So \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -3\sin(\log x) + 4\cos(\log x)\).

Differentiate \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) with respect to \(x\):
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = \dfrac{dy}{dx} + x\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).

Also
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[-3\sin(\log x) + 4\cos(\log x)\right] = -3\cos(\log x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} - 4\sin(\log x)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x}\left[-3\cos(\log x) - 4\sin(\log x)\right] = -\dfrac{y}{x}\).

Hence
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + x\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\dfrac{y}{x}\).

Multiply through by \(x\):
\(x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -y\), i.e. \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\).

This is the standard Cauchy-Euler form. (The equation as printed in the book shows \(x\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) as its first term, an apparent misprint for \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).) Hence the function is a solution of the intended equation.

solution:
The equation is

\(y\left(1 + \log x\right)\dfrac{dx}{dy} - x\log x = 0\)

that is,

\(y\left(1 + \log x\right)\dfrac{dx}{dy} = x\log x\)

**Step 1: separate the variables.** Cross-multiplying,

\(y\left(1 + \log x\right)dx = x\log x\,dy\)

\(\dfrac{1 + \log x}{x\log x}\,dx = \dfrac{dy}{y}\)

**Step 2: integrate both sides.** For the left-hand side put

\(u = x\log x\)

Then, by the product rule,

\(du = \left(\log x \cdot 1 + x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx = \left(1 + \log x\right)dx\)

which is exactly the numerator, so

\(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1 + \log x}{x\log x}\,dx = \int\dfrac{du}{u} = \log|u| = \log\left|x\log x\right|\)

and \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dy}{y} = \log|y|\). Writing the constant of integration as \(\log|k|\),

\(\log\left|x\log x\right| = \log|y| + \log|k|\)

\(\log\left|x\log x\right| = \log|ky|\)

\(x\log x = k\,y\)   (general solution)

**Step 3: apply the condition \(x = e,\ y = e^{2}\).** Since \(\log e = 1\),

\(e \times 1 = k\,e^{2}\)

\(k = \dfrac{1}{e}\)

**Particular solution.**

\(x\log x = \dfrac{y}{e}\)

\(y = e\,x\log x\)

**Verification.** With \(y = e\,x\log x\),

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e\left(\log x + 1\right)\)  so  \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{1}{e\left(1 + \log x\right)}\)

Substituting into the left-hand side of the original equation,

\(y\left(1 + \log x\right)\dfrac{dx}{dy} - x\log x = e\,x\log x\left(1 + \log x\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{e\left(1 + \log x\right)} - x\log x = x\log x - x\log x = 0\)

and at \(x = e\), \(y = e \cdot e \cdot \log e = e^{2}\), so the initial condition is met as well.

solution:
The relation \(y^2 = (x + c)^3\) has one arbitrary constant \(c\), so differentiate once and eliminate \(c\).

Differentiate with respect to \(x\):
\(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3(x + c)^2\). \(\quad(1)\)

From the given equation, \((x + c)^3 = y^2\), so \((x + c) = y^{2/3}\) and \((x + c)^2 = y^{4/3}\).

To eliminate \((x+c)\), cube \((1)\) and use the original equation:

Cube \((1)\): \(\left(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 27(x + c)^6 = 27\big[(x + c)^3\big]^2 = 27(y^2)^2 = 27y^4\).

\(\therefore 8y^3\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 27y^4\).

Divide by \(y^3\):
\(8\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 27y\).

\(\therefore\) the required differential equation is \(8\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = 27y\).

solution:
Let \(x\) be the mass of the Bismath present at time \(t\).
Then \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -k \cdot x\) where \(k > 0\)
Solving the differential equation, we get
\(x = c \cdot e^{-kt}\)  ... (1)
where \(c\) is constant of proportionality.
Given that \(x = 800\), when \(t = 0\)
using these values in equation (1), we get
\(800 = c \cdot 1 = c\)
\(x = 800\, e^{-kt}\)  ... (2)
Since half life is 5 days, we have \(x = 400\) when \(t = 5\),
From equation (2), we have
\(400 = 800\, e^{-5k}\)
\(e^{-5k} = \dfrac{400}{800} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  ... (3)
Now we have determine \(x\), when \(t = 30\),
From equation (2), we have
\(x = 800\, e^{-30k} = 800\left(e^{-5k}\right)^6 = 800 \cdot \dfrac{1}{64} = 12.5\)
The mass after 30 days will be \(12.5\) mg.
note: The step e^{-30k} = (e^{-5k})^6 = 1/64 was missing and a stray '(verify!)' was printed.
